The letter developed in medieval Latin-script writing from a doubled form of the letter represented in modern typography by ⟨u⟩ or ⟨v⟩, which were not yet consistently distinguished as separate letters. The doubled form was used to represent the Germanic sound /w/, for which Classical Latin had no separate letter, and gradually developed into the independent letter ⟨w⟩. Its Norwegian name, dobbelt-v (“double v”), refers to its shape and historical origin. / The uppercase form of w. The letter developed in medieval Latin-script writing from a doubling of the letter forms ⟨u⟩ or ⟨v⟩, which were not yet consistently distinguished as separate letters. From stor (“great”) + fyrste (“prince”), literally “great prince”. The title corresponds to Russian вели́кий кня́зь (velíkij knjázʹ, “grand prince”), likewise literally “great prince”. The first element stor (“great”) is from Old Norse stórr (“big, great”), from Proto-Germanic *stōraz (“big, large”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”). The second element fyrste (“prince”) is from Middle Low German vurste (“prince; first”), from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Ny

13615.etyen:
Related to fange (“to catch, capture”) and få (“to get, receive”), and compare dialectal Swedish fakksa. These belong to the Germanic word-family represented by *fanhaną (“to catch, seize”).
The deeper origin of the Proto-Germanic verb is uncertain. It has been derived either from a nasal-infix formation of *peh₂ḱ- (“to secure, attach, strengthen”), or from a Pre-Germanic formation ultimately involving *h₂pó (“off, away”) and *h₂n(e)ḱ- (“to reach, attain”). / Borrowed from German fachen, a technical term in traditional felt-hat manufacture; compare fakk (“loose mass of hair or wool prepared for felting”), itself borrowed from German Fach.
The associated German noun Fach is from Proto-Germanic *faką (“defined or enclosed space; compartment”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ- (“to fit, fasten, fix”).

1000239.etyen:
Unadapted borrowing from Portuguese morna (“morna”), but ultimately of uncertain origin.
The name of the Cape Verdean musical genre is marna (“morna”) (also morna) in Kabuverdianu and morna (“morna”) in Portuguese. The ultimate origin of the term is disputed. One common proposal connects it with Portuguese morna, the feminine form of morno (“lukewarm, mild”), perhaps in reference to the slow, mellow character of the music. Other proposals connect the term with English mourn (“to grieve”) or French morne (“gloomy, dreary”); none of these explanations is securely established.

1002799.etyen:
Named after Queen Maud of Norway (1869–1938), wife of King Haakon VII. The name dates from the Norwegian exploration and mapping of the area during the third Norvegia expedition of 1929–1930, led by Hjalmar Riiser-Larsen with Finn Lützow-Holm as one of the expedition's aviators. The name, originally applied to land explored during these expeditions, was subsequently used for the wider Norwegian Antarctic territory annexed on 14 January 1939. Literally “Queen Maud Land”.
